Appendix A Detailed derivation and properties of blurred sampling

In this section, we derive the blurred sampling procedure and prove the properties stated in the main text. Blurred sampling does not modify the original sampler, which generates configurations 𝒙{\bm{x}} distributed according to p⁡(𝒙)p({\bm{x}}). Throughout this section, we denote by 𝒙{\bm{x}} samples drawn from pp, and by 𝒙′{\bm{x}}^{\prime} the configuration obtained after the post-processing step.

A.1 Unit expectation of the reweighting factor

We first verify that the reweighting factors have unit expectation, i.e., ⟨ω⁡(𝒙′)⟩r=1{\left<\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{r}=1, for the general blur kernel defined in Eq. (6). Since K⁡(𝒙′|𝒙)K({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}}) is a Markov kernel, ∑𝒙′r⁡(𝒙′)=∑𝒙′∑𝒙K⁡(𝒙′,𝒙)​p​(𝒙)=∑𝒙p⁡(𝒙)\sum_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}r({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=\sum_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}\sum_{{\bm{x}}}K({\bm{x}}^{\prime},{\bm{x}})p({\bm{x}})=\sum_{\bm{x}}p({\bm{x}}), and hence rr is normalized whenever pp is normalized. The reweighting factor is defined as ω⁡(𝒙′)=p⁡(𝒙′)/r⁡(𝒙′)\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})/r({\bm{x}}^{\prime}). Therefore,

⟨ω⁡(𝒙′)⟩r=∑𝒙′r⁡(𝒙′)​p​(𝒙′)/r⁡(𝒙′)=∑𝒙′p⁡(𝒙′)=1.{\left<\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{r}=\sum_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}r({\bm{x}}^{\prime})p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})/r({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=\sum_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=1. (18)

A.2 Finite-sample unbiased estimators

We first construct the finite-sample unbiased estimator for expectation values under the original distribution pp. Since ⟨ω⟩r=1{\left<\omega\right>}_{r}=1, we have

⟨A⟩p=⟨ω​A⟩r⟨ω⟩r=⟨ω​A⟩r.{\left<A\right>}_{p}=\frac{{\left<\omega A\right>}_{r}}{{\left<\omega\right>}_{r}}={\left<\omega A\right>}_{r}. (19)

Therefore, the finite size estimator

⟨A⟩p^=1N​∑i=1Nω⁡(𝒙i′)​A​(𝒙i′)≡[ω​A]r\widehat{{\left<A\right>}_{p}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime}_{i})A({\bm{x}}^{\prime}_{i})\equiv[\omega A]_{r} (20)

is an unbiased estimator for ⟨A⟩p{\left<A\right>}_{p} with 𝔼⁡[⟨A⟩p^]=⟨A⟩p\mathbb{E}[{\widehat{{\left<A\right>}_{p}}}]={\left<A\right>}_{p}.

For covariance-type quantities ⟨⟨A,B⟩⟩p≡⟨A​B⟩p−⟨A⟩p​⟨B⟩p{\left<{\left<A,B\right>}\right>}_{p}\equiv{\left<AB\right>}_{p}-{\left<A\right>}_{p}{\left<B\right>}_{p}, we use the identities ⟨A​B⟩p=⟨ω​A​B⟩r,⟨A⟩p=⟨ω​A⟩r,⟨B⟩p=⟨ω​B⟩r{\left<AB\right>}_{p}={\left<\omega AB\right>}_{r},{\left<A\right>}_{p}={\left<\omega A\right>}_{r},{\left<B\right>}_{p}={\left<\omega B\right>}_{r}. Hence,

⟨⟨A,B⟩⟩p=⟨ω​A​B⟩r−⟨ω​A⟩r​⟨ω​B⟩r{\left<{\left<A,B\right>}\right>}_{p}={\left<\omega AB\right>}_{r}-{\left<\omega A\right>}_{r}{\left<\omega B\right>}_{r} (21)

We now use the identity ⟨ω⟩r=1{\left<\omega\right>}_{r}=1 to rewrite the first term as ⟨ω​A​B⟩r=⟨ω⟩r​⟨ω​A​B⟩r{\left<\omega AB\right>}_{r}={\left<\omega\right>}_{r}\,{\left<\omega AB\right>}_{r}, and add–subtract ⟨ω2​A​B⟩r{\left<\omega^{2}AB\right>}_{r}:

⟨⟨A,B⟩⟩p=⟨ω⟩r​⟨ω​A​B⟩r−⟨ω2​A​B⟩r−⟨ω​A⟩r​⟨ω​B⟩r+⟨ω2​A​B⟩r=⟨⟨ω​A,ω​B⟩⟩r−⟨⟨ω,ω​A​B⟩⟩r.\begin{split}{\left<{\left<A,B\right>}\right>}_{p}&={\left<\omega\right>}_{r}{\left<\omega AB\right>}_{r}-{\left<\omega^{2}AB\right>}_{r}\\ &-{\left<\omega A\right>}_{r}{\left<\omega B\right>}_{r}+{\left<\omega^{2}AB\right>}_{r}\\ &={\left<{\left<\omega A,\omega B\right>}\right>}_{r}-{\left<{\left<\omega,\omega AB\right>}\right>}_{r}.\end{split} (22)

It is well known that the finite-sample unbiased estimator of the covariance ⟨⟨X1,X2⟩⟩r{\left<{\left<X_{1},X_{2}\right>}\right>}_{r} is

⟨⟨X1,X2⟩⟩^r=NN−1​([X1​X2]r−[X1]r​[X2]r).\widehat{{\left<{\left<X_{1},X_{2}\right>}\right>}}_{r}=\frac{N}{N-1}\left({\left[X_{1}X_{2}\right]}_{r}-{\left[X_{1}\right]}_{r}\,{\left[X_{2}\right]}_{r}\right). (23)

Therefore we have that

⟨⟨A,B⟩⟩^p=⟨⟨ω​A,ω​B⟩⟩^r−⟨⟨ω,ω​A​B⟩⟩^r=NN−1×([ω]r​[ω​A​B]r−[ω​A]r​[ω​B]r)=N​[ω]r2N−1×([ω​A​B]r[ω]r−[ω​A]r[ω]r​[ω​B]r[ω]r),\begin{split}\widehat{{\left<{\left<A,B\right>}\right>}}_{p}&=\widehat{{\left<{\left<\omega A,\omega B\right>}\right>}}_{r}-\widehat{{\left<{\left<\omega,\omega AB\right>}\right>}}_{r}\\ &=\frac{N}{N-1}\times\left({\left[\omega\right]}_{r}\,{\left[\omega AB\right]}_{r}-{\left[\omega A\right]}_{r}\,{\left[\omega B\right]}_{r}\right)\\ &=\frac{N\,{\left[\omega\right]}_{r}^{2}}{N-1}\times\left(\frac{{\left[\omega AB\right]}_{r}}{{\left[\omega\right]}_{r}}-\frac{{\left[\omega A\right]}_{r}}{{\left[\omega\right]}_{r}}\frac{{\left[\omega B\right]}_{r}}{{\left[\omega\right]}_{r}}\right),\end{split} (24)

is the finite-sample unbiased estimator for ⟨⟨A,B⟩⟩p{\left<{\left<A,B\right>}\right>}_{p}.

In practice, one typically employs the self-normalized estimator (i.e., the right-hand side of the last line in Eq. (24)), which is a biased estimator. However, this bias manifests itself as a common multiplicative factor affecting all covariance-like quantities. Since the SR/TDVP update depends only on ratios of such quantities (e.g., through 𝑺−1​𝑭\bm{S}^{-1}\bm{F}), this common factor cancels in the parameter update. Consequently, the resulting time evolution is unaffected by this overall factor.

A.3 Bound of the reweighting factor and effective sample size

Consider the distribution obtained after marginalizing the kernel KK in Eq. (6):

r⁡(𝒙′)=∑𝒙K⁡(𝒙′|𝒙)​p​(𝒙)=∑𝒙((1−q)​δ𝒙′,𝒙​p​(𝒙)+q​Koff​(𝒙′|𝒙)​p​(𝒙))=(1−q)​p​(𝒙′)+q​∑𝒙Koff​(𝒙′|𝒙)​p​(𝒙).\begin{split}r({\bm{x}}^{\prime})&=\sum_{{\bm{x}}}K({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}})p({\bm{x}})\\ &=\sum_{{\bm{x}}}\left((1-q)\,\delta_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime},{\bm{x}}}p({\bm{x}})+q\,K_{\mathrm{off}}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}})p({\bm{x}})\right)\\ &=(1-q)p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})+q\,\sum_{{\bm{x}}}K_{\mathrm{off}}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}})p({\bm{x}}).\end{split} (25)

Since Koff​(𝒙′|𝒙)​p​(𝒙)≥0K_{\mathrm{off}}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}})p({\bm{x}})\geq 0, we see that

r⁡(𝒙′)≥(1−q)​p​(𝒙′).r({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\geq(1-q)p({\bm{x}}^{\prime}). (26)

As a result, the reweighting factor is bounded by

ω⁡(𝒙′)=p⁡(𝒙′)r⁡(𝒙′)≤p⁡(𝒙′)(1−q)​p​(𝒙′)=11−q.\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=\frac{p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})}{r({\bm{x}}^{\prime})}\leq\frac{p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})}{(1-q)p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})}=\frac{1}{1-q}. (27)

Using the fact that p⁡(𝒙′)≥0p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\geq 0, we conclude that the reweighting factor is bounded as

0≤ω⁡(𝒙′)≤11−q.0\leq\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\leq\frac{1}{1-q}. (28)

Since the reweighting factors satisfy ω⁡(𝒙)∈[0,11−q]\omega({\bm{x}})\in[0,\frac{1}{1-q}], we have the pointwise inequality

ω​(𝒙)2≤11−q​ω​(𝒙).\omega({\bm{x}})^{2}\leq\frac{1}{1-q}\omega({\bm{x}}). (29)

Taking expectations with respect to rr yields

⟨ω2​(𝒙′)⟩r≤11−q​⟨ω⁡(𝒙′)⟩r.\displaystyle{\left<\omega^{2}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{r}\leq\frac{1}{1-q}{\left<\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{r}. (30)

Using ⟨ω⁡(𝒙′)⟩r=1{\left<\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{r}=1, we obtain

ESS⁡[ω]=⟨ω⁡(𝒙′)⟩r2/⟨ω​(𝒙′)2⟩r≥1−q.\displaystyle\mathrm{ESS}[\omega]={\left<\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{r}^{2}/{\left<\omega({\bm{x}}^{\prime})^{2}\right>}_{r}\geq 1-q. (31)

A.4 Randomized blur construction

For the randomized generalization of blurred sampling, we first recall the construction. Let Kλ{K_{\lambda}} be a family of blur kernels parameterized by λ\lambda, where each kernel satisfies the structure of Eq. (6) and has sparse connectivity. For each sample 𝒙i∼p⁡(𝒙){\bm{x}}_{i}\sim p({\bm{x}}), we independently draw λi∼f⁡(λ)\lambda_{i}\sim f(\lambda) from a normalized density ff, and then generate 𝒙i′∼Kλi(⋅|𝒙i){\bm{x}}^{\prime}_{i}\sim K_{\lambda_{i}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}_{i}). Let rλ​(𝒙′)=∑𝒙p⁡(𝒙)​Kλ​(𝒙′|𝒙)r_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=\sum_{{\bm{x}}}p({\bm{x}})K_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}}) denote the blurred distribution corresponding to a fixed λ\lambda. We define the conditional reweighting factor ωλ​(𝒙′)=p⁡(𝒙′)rλ​(𝒙′)\omega_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=\frac{p({\bm{x}}^{\prime})}{r_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})}. Then the estimator [ωλ​A]f⁡(λ)​rλ{\left[\omega_{\lambda}A\right]}_{f(\lambda)r_{\lambda}} remains finite-sample unbiased and equal to ⟨A⟩p{\left<A\right>}_{p},

⟨A⁡(𝒙)⟩p=⟨⟨ωλ​(𝒙′)​A​(𝒙′)⟩rλ⟩f⁡(λ)=⟨ωλ​(𝒙′)​A​(𝒙′)⟩f⁡(λ)​rλ,{\left<A({\bm{x}})\right>}_{p}={\left<{\left<\omega_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})A({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{r_{\lambda}}\right>}_{f(\lambda)}={\left<\omega_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})A({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right>}_{f(\lambda){r_{\lambda}}}, (32)

provided that no support-mismatch pathology occurs. Similarly, the estimator in Eq. (11) also applies under randomized blurred sampling, with [ω⋅]r{\left[\omega\cdot\right]}_{r} replaced by [ωλ⋅]f⁡(λ)​rλ​(𝒙′){\left[\omega_{\lambda}\cdot\right]}_{f(\lambda)r_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})}. As a direct application, the probabilistic blur construction can be used to refine the continuum kernel introduced in Eq. (8), where the displacement magnitude ϵ\epsilon and coordinate directions 𝐞α\mathbf{e}_{\alpha} are treated as random parameters λ\lambda. By sampling these quantities from suitable distributions, the resulting blur approaches an effective Gaussian kernel. In particular, this randomization restores rotational symmetry at the level of the induced proposal distribution.

A.5 QGT estimator from randomized blurred sampling

Although the marginal distribution of 𝒙′{\bm{x}}^{\prime} is r⁡(𝒙′)=∑λf⁡(λ)​rλ​(𝒙′)r({\bm{x}}^{\prime})=\sum_{\lambda}f(\lambda)\,r_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}), which coincides with that induced by the average kernel Kmix​(𝒙′|𝒙)=∑λf⁡(λ)​Kλ​(𝒙′|𝒙)K_{\mathrm{mix}}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}})=\sum_{\lambda}f(\lambda)\,K_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}}), the present construction differs in how the reweighting factor is evaluated. In our scheme, the weight is evaluated conditionally on the realized value of λ\lambda, i.e., with respect to rλ​(𝒙′)r_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}) rather than the marginal r⁡(𝒙′)r({\bm{x}}^{\prime}). As a result, the computational cost remains governed by the sparsity of each individual kernel KλK_{\lambda}, rather than by the mixed kernel KmixK_{\mathrm{mix}}, which can be difficult to calculate or require an auxiliary Monte Carlo calculation. This randomized formulation therefore represents a trade-off: while it does not fully expand the support at the level of individual blur kernels, it preserves sparsity and remains computationally feasible in regimes where the deterministic construction becomes costly. As demonstrated in Sec. IV.3, randomized blurred sampling successfully resolves cases in which Hamiltonian-induced blurred sampling fails to cure the QGT instability.

While the randomized formulation preserves sparsity and improves robustness in practice, its impact on the QGT estimator can be characterized more precisely. In particular, although the marginal distribution r⁡(𝒙′)r({\bm{x}}^{\prime}) may explore the full Hilbert space, the reweighting factor is evaluated conditionally on the realized value of λ\lambda, namely with respect to rλ​(𝒙′)r_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}). This conditioning leads to a modified structure of the QGT estimator, which we now make explicit. For convenience, we denote by suppλ{\text{supp}}_{\lambda} the support of the conditional distribution rλ​(𝒙′)r_{\lambda}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}). We further introduce the indicator function

ℐλ​(𝒙)={1,if ​𝒙∈suppλ,0,otherwise.\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}({\bm{x}})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }{\bm{x}}\in{\text{supp}}_{\lambda},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (33)

In the infinite-sample limit, the QGT estimator obtained from randomized blurred sampling reads

Si​jr-blur=⟨∑𝒙ℐλ​(𝒙)​⟨∂θiψ𝜽|𝒙⟩​⟨𝒙|∂θjψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩⟩λ−⟨∂θiψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩​⟨ψ𝜽|∂θjψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩=∑𝒙⟨ℐλ​(𝒙)⟩λ​⟨∂θiψ𝜽|𝒙⟩​⟨𝒙|∂θjψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩−⟨∂θiψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩​⟨ψ𝜽|∂θjψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩.\begin{split}S_{ij}^{\text{r-blur}}&={\left<\frac{\sum_{{\bm{x}}}\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}({\bm{x}})\braket{\partial_{\theta_{i}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\bm{x}}}\braket{{\bm{x}}|\partial_{\theta_{j}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}\right>}_{\lambda}-\frac{\braket{\partial_{\theta_{i}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}\frac{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|\partial_{\theta_{j}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}\\ &=\frac{\sum_{{\bm{x}}}{\left<\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}({\bm{x}})\right>}_{\lambda}\braket{\partial_{\theta_{i}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\bm{x}}}\braket{{\bm{x}}|\partial_{\theta_{j}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}-\frac{\braket{\partial_{\theta_{i}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}\frac{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|\partial_{\theta_{j}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}.\end{split} (34)

Compared with the exact QGT in Eq. (1), the deviation is

Δ​Si​j=∑𝒙⟨1−ℐλ​(𝒙)⟩λ​⟨∂θiψ𝜽|𝒙⟩​⟨𝒙|∂θjψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩.\Delta S_{ij}=\frac{\sum_{{\bm{x}}}{\left<1-\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}({\bm{x}})\right>}_{\lambda}\braket{\partial_{\theta_{i}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\bm{x}}}\braket{{\bm{x}}|\partial_{\theta_{j}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}. (35)

Therefore, the estimator deviates from the exact QGT whenever ⟨ℐλ​(𝒙)⟩λ≠1{\left<\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}({\bm{x}})\right>}_{\lambda}\neq 1.

Importantly, this deviation does not necessarily invalidate the resulting dynamics. We now show that, provided the variational ansatz is sufficiently expressive, randomized blurred sampling yields the exact projected TDVP evolution, despite modifying the QGT. The key observation is that the induced modification can be interpreted as a positive deformation of the Hilbert-space metric entering the TDVP principle.

Recall that the TDVP equation in Eq. (2) arises from minimizing the Hilbert-space distance between the variational tangent vector and the exact time-evolution direction. In the tangent space, these directions are given by

|ψ𝜽˙⟩var=(1−|ψ𝜽⟩​⟨ψ𝜽|⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩)​∑i|∂θiψ𝜽⟩​θi˙⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩|ψ𝜽˙⟩exact=(1−|ψ𝜽⟩​⟨ψ𝜽|⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩)​−ξ​H^​|ψ𝜽⟩⟨ψ𝜽|ψ𝜽⟩.\begin{split}\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{var}}&=\left(1-\frac{\ket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\bra{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}\right)\frac{\sum_{i}\ket{\partial_{\theta_{i}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\dot{\theta_{i}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}\\ \ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{exact}}&=\left(1-\frac{\ket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}\bra{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}\right)\frac{-\xi\hat{H}\ket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}{\braket{{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}|{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}}.\\ \end{split} (36)

The TDVP equation follows from minimizing the distance between these two tangent vectors,

ℒ=‖|ψ𝜽˙⟩var−|ψ𝜽˙⟩exact‖,\mathcal{L}=||\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{var}}-\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{exact}}||, (37)

where the distance is defined through the Hilbert-space norm ||⋅||≡∑𝒙|⋅(𝒙)|2||\cdot||\equiv\sum_{\bm{x}}|\cdot({\bm{x}})|^{2}.

If we replace the standard Hilbert-space norm by the weighted norm ||⋅||′≡∑𝒙⟨ℐλ(𝒙)⟩λ|⋅(𝒙)|2||\cdot||^{\prime}\equiv\sum_{\bm{x}}{\left<\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}({\bm{x}})\right>}_{\lambda}|\cdot({\bm{x}})|^{2}, the resulting TDVP equation reproduces precisely the QGT obtained from randomized blurred sampling. This modification is therefore equivalent to a deformation of the underlying Hilbert-space metric. By construction, ⟨ℐλ​(𝒙)⟩λ>0{\left<\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}({\bm{x}})\right>}_{\lambda}>0 for all 𝒙{\bm{x}}, so the weighted norm remains strictly positive definite. Consequently,

‖|ψ𝜽˙⟩var−|ψ𝜽˙⟩exact‖=0⇔‖|ψ𝜽˙⟩var−|ψ𝜽˙⟩exact‖′=0.||\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{var}}-\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{exact}}||=0\,\Leftrightarrow\,||\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{var}}-\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{exact}}||^{\prime}=0. (38)

Therefore, if the variational ansatz is sufficiently expressive—namely, if there exists a parameter velocity 𝜽˙∗\dot{\bm{\theta}}^{*} such that ‖|ψ𝜽˙⟩var−|ψ𝜽˙⟩exact‖=0||\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{var}}-\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{exact}}||=0, then the same 𝜽˙∗\dot{\bm{\theta}}^{*} also solves the TDVP equation defined with the modified norm, ‖|ψ𝜽˙⟩var−|ψ𝜽˙⟩exact‖′=0||\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{var}}-\ket{\dot{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}_{\mathrm{exact}}||^{\prime}=0 and vice versa. Hence, randomized blurred sampling yields the correct parameter dynamics whenever the variational ansatz is sufficiently expressive.

In contrast, under support mismatch the standard VMC QGT corresponds to a deformation of the Hilbert-space metric with vanishing weights on configurations that are not sampled. The resulting metric therefore develops null directions and becomes degenerate, leading to potentially spurious dynamics even when the variational ansatz is sufficiently expressive. Randomized blurred sampling removes this degeneracy. Although the resulting QGT differs from the exact one, the induced metric remains strictly positive definite and spans the correct tangent directions. In this sense, randomized blurred sampling acts as a natural regularization of the QGT, restoring stability while preserving the correct projected dynamics.

Appendix B Details of the parity mixing problem in TFIM

We study the dynamics of the initial state chosen as the equal-weight superposition of computational-basis states with even ZZ-parity,

|ψ0⟩=∑𝒙𝒫^Z+12​|𝒙⟩,\ket{\psi_{0}}=\sum_{{\bm{x}}}\frac{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}+1}{2}\ket{{\bm{x}}}, (39)

where 𝒫^Z≡∏i=1NZi\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}\equiv\prod_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i} denotes the ZZ-parity operator and |𝒙⟩\ket{{\bm{x}}} are computational-basis states with xi∈{±1}x_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}. The time evolution is governed by the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) Hamiltonian,

H^TFIM=J​∑i=1NZi​Zi+1+h​∑i=1NXi,\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}=J\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}Z_{i+1}+h\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}, (40)

where periodic boundary conditions are assumed. In this setup, we are interested in how the ZZ-parity evolves under the dynamics, characterized by

𝒫Z​(t)=⟨ψ0|ei​H^TFIM​t​𝒫Z^​e−i​H^TFIM​t|ψ0⟩⟨ψ0|ψ0⟩.\mathcal{P}_{Z}(t)=\frac{\braket{\psi_{0}|e^{i\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}t}\hat{\mathcal{P}_{Z}}e^{-i\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}t}|\psi_{0}}}{\braket{\psi_{0}|\psi_{0}}}. (41)

In the following, we describe the variational ansätze employed—including the RBM and Gaussian ansatz—and present the analytic solution.

B.1 RBM ansatz and its initialization

We employ a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) with complex-valued parameters as the variational ansatz. The wavefunction is given by

ψRBM​(𝒙)=exp⁡(∑i=1Nai​xi)​∏j=1M2​cosh⁡(bj+∑i=1NWi​j​xi).\psi_{\mathrm{RBM}}({\bm{x}})=\exp\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}x_{i}\right)\prod_{j=1}^{M}2\cosh\left(b_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}W_{ij}x_{i}\right). (42)

where aia_{i}, bjb_{j}, and Wi​jW_{ij} are complex parameters, and MM denotes the number of hidden units. We define the ansatz size as α≡M/N\alpha\equiv M/N. The initialization is particularly simple. The action of the parity projector on a computational-basis state can be written as

𝒫^Z+12|𝒙⟩=cos(π4(N−∑i=1Nxi))2|𝒙⟩.\frac{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}+1}{2}\ket{{\bm{x}}}=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}(N-\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i})\right)^{2}\ket{{\bm{x}}}. (43)

Choosing the RBM parameters as ai=0a_{i}=0, b1=b2=i​π​N/4b_{1}=b_{2}=\mathrm{i}{\pi N}/{4}, Wi​1=Wi​2=−i⁡(π/4)W_{i1}=W_{i2}=-\mathrm{i}(\pi/4) (with all other parameters set to zero), the RBM wavefunction exactly reproduces these amplitudes, thereby initializing the variational state to the chosen parity sector. For numerical stability, we add a small perturbation of order 10−310^{-3} to the parameters, ensuring that the logarithmic derivatives remain well defined.

B.2 Exact solution via mapping to Majorana fermions

It is well known that the one-dimensional TFIM can be mapped to a system of free fermions. Here we follow the mapping of Ref. [91] and directly introduce 2​N2N Majorana fermions γ2​i,γ2​i+1\gamma_{2i},\gamma_{2i+1}. The spin operators are represented as

Zi+1=(−i)iγ0γ1γ2⋯γ2​i,Xi+1=−iγ2​iγ2​i+1.Z_{i+1}=(-\mathrm{i})^{i}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\cdots\gamma_{2i},\,\,X_{i+1}=-\mathrm{i}\gamma_{2i}\gamma_{2i+1}. (44)

One then obtains

Zi​Zi+1={−i​γ2​i−1​γ2​i,for ​i<N,i​𝒫^X​γ2​N−1​γ0,for ​i=N.Z_{i}Z_{i+1}=\begin{cases}-\mathrm{i}\,\gamma_{2i-1}\gamma_{2i},&\text{for }i<N,\\ \mathrm{i}\,\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{X}\,\gamma_{2N-1}\gamma_{0},&\text{for }i=N.\end{cases} (45)

where 𝒫^X=∏Xi\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{X}=\prod X_{i} is the conserved XX-parity operator. For even system size NN, the initial state |ψ0⟩\ket{\psi_{0}} lies in the sector 𝒫^X=1\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{X}=1. Restricting to this sector, the Hamiltonian becomes

H^TFIM=−iJ∑i=0N−2γ2​i+1γ2​i+2+iJγ2​N−1γ0−ih∑iγ2​iγ2​i+1.\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}=-\mathrm{i}J\sum_{i=0}^{N-2}\gamma_{2i+1}\gamma_{2i+2}+\mathrm{i}J\gamma_{2N-1}\gamma_{0}-\mathrm{i}h\sum_{i}\gamma_{2i}\gamma_{2i+1}. (46)

In this representation, the ZZ-parity operator reads

𝒫=(−i)N/2​∏i=0N/2−1γ4​i+1​γ4​i+2.\mathcal{P}=(-\mathrm{i})^{N/2}\prod_{i=0}^{N/2-1}\gamma_{4i+1}\gamma_{4i+2}. (47)

Although the Hamiltonian is quadratic in Majorana operators, so that the time-evolution operator is a fermionic Gaussian operator (a matchgate circuit), the initial state |ψ0⟩\ket{\psi_{0}} is not Gaussian. We therefore exploit the symmetry of the ZZ-parity operator. Using the anticommutation relation {Xi,𝒫^Z}=0\{X_{i},\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}\}=0, which implies

𝒫^Z​H^TFIM​(J,h)=H^TFIM​(J,−h)​𝒫^Z,\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,h)=\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,-h)\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}, (48)

we obtain

|ψ⁡(t)⟩≡e−i​H^TFIM​(J,h)​t​|ψ0⟩=e−i​H^TFIM​(J,h)​t​𝒫^Z+12​|+⟩=12​e−i​H^TFIM​(J,h)​t​|+⟩+𝒫^Z2​e−i​H^TFIM​(J,−h)​t​|+⟩.\begin{split}\ket{\psi(t)}&\equiv e^{-i\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,h)t}\ket{\psi_{0}}\\ &=e^{-i\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,h)t}\frac{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}+1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{+}\\ &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{-i\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,h)t}\ket{+}+\frac{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}}{\sqrt{2}}e^{-i\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,-h)t}\ket{+}.\end{split} (49)

Since the state |+⟩\ket{+} is Gaussian—being the ground state of the quadratic Hamiltonian −∑iXi=∑iiγ2​iγ2​i+1-\sum_{i}X_{i}=\sum_{i}\mathrm{i}\gamma_{2i}\gamma_{2i+1}. Its time evolution under the quadratic TFIM Hamiltonian remains Gaussian. We denote e−i​H^TFIM​(J,h)​t​|+⟩e^{-i\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,h)t}\ket{+} as |ψG+​(J,h,t)⟩\ket{\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,h,t)}. The full wavefunction can then be written as

|ψ⁡(t)⟩=12​|ψG+​(J,h,t)⟩+𝒫^Z2​|ψG+​(J,−h,t)⟩.\ket{\psi(t)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,h,t)}+\frac{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,-h,t)}. (50)

The time-dependent ZZ-parity becomes:

𝒫Z​(t)=R​e​⟨ψG+​(J,−h,t)|ψG+​(J,h,t)⟩+12​⟨ψG+​(J,h,t)|𝒫^Z|ψG+​(J,h,t)⟩+12​⟨ψG+​(J,−h,t)|𝒫^Z|ψG+​(J,−h,t)⟩.\begin{split}\mathcal{P}_{Z}(t)&={\mathrm{R}e}\braket{\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,-h,t)|\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,h,t)}\\ &+\frac{1}{2}\braket{\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,h,t)|\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}|\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,h,t)}\\ &+\frac{1}{2}\braket{\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,-h,t)|\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}|\psi_{\text{G}}^{+}(J,-h,t)}.\end{split} (51)

The problem thus reduces to evaluating (i) the overlap between two Gaussian states and (ii) the expectation value of 𝒫^Z\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z} in a Gaussian state. The overlap of two general fermionic Gaussian states (without U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry) can be computed using Pfaffian techniques; we refer the interested reader to Ref. [90] for details. The operator 𝒫^Z\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z} is a product of Majorana operators [cf. Eq. (47)], and its expectation value in a Gaussian state can be expressed as a Pfaffian of the corresponding covariance matrix Gi,j≡⟨γi​γj⟩G_{i,j}\equiv\braket{\gamma_{i}\gamma_{j}} as

⟨∏iγαi⟩=pf​[Gαi,αj].\braket{\prod_{i}\gamma_{\alpha_{i}}}=\text{pf}\left[G_{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}}\right]. (52)

Therefore, the time evolution of the ZZ-parity can be computed analytically for system sizes far beyond the reach of exact diagonalization.

B.3 Gaussian ansatz and its initialization

As shown in the main text, the RBM ansatz combined with blurred sampling performs well up to system sizes N∼8N\sim 8, where we employ a relatively large network with α=4\alpha=4. For larger systems, however, the expressiveness of the ansatz becomes the primary bottleneck of the t-VMC approach. To disentangle this limitation from other algorithmic aspects of t-VMC, we consider an alternative Gaussian ansatz. This ansatz permits efficient evaluation of wavefunction amplitudes and is capable of representing the exact time-evolved state |ψ⁡(t)⟩\ket{\psi(t)} at all times:

|ψGaussian⟩=|G1⟩+𝒫^Z​|G2⟩,\ket{\psi_{\text{Gaussian}}}=\ket{G^{1}}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}\ket{G^{2}}, (53)

where |G1⟩\ket{G^{1}} and |G2⟩\ket{G^{2}} are Gaussian states parameterized as

|G1,2⟩=eθi​j1,2​γi​γj​|+⟩,\ket{G^{1,2}}=e^{\theta^{1,2}_{ij}\gamma_{i}\gamma_{j}}\ket{+}, (54)

with parameters θ1,2\theta^{1,2} being 2​N×2​N2N\times 2N antisymmetric real matrices, each containing N⁡(2​N−1)N(2N-1) independent parameters.

The remaining task is to evaluate the amplitudes in the computational basis,

⟨𝒙|ψGaussian⟩=⟨𝒙|G1⟩+𝒫^Z​⟨𝒙|G2⟩.\braket{{\bm{x}}|\psi_{\text{Gaussian}}}=\braket{{\bm{x}}|G^{1}}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{Z}\braket{{\bm{x}}|G^{2}}. (55)

However, the basis state |𝒙⟩\ket{{\bm{x}}} is not Gaussian. Importantly, the wavefunction should preserves the XX-parity, so that ⟨𝒙|ψGaussian⟩\braket{{\bm{x}}|\psi_{\text{Gaussian}}} should be the same as ⟨𝒫^X​𝒙|ψGaussian⟩\braket{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{X}{\bm{x}}|\psi_{\text{Gaussian}}}. Consequently, we may work in the symmetric combination

|𝒙⟩+≡12​|𝒙⟩+12​|𝒫^X​𝒙⟩\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{+}\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{{\bm{x}}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{X}{\bm{x}}} (56)

which is a Gaussian state. In fact, |𝒙⟩+\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{+} is the ground state of the quadratic Majorana Hamiltonian

i​∑i=0N−2xi+1​xi+2​γ2​i+1​γ2​i+2−i​xN​x1​γ2​N−1​γ0.\mathrm{i}\sum_{i=0}^{N-2}x_{i+1}x_{i+2}\gamma_{2i+1}\gamma_{2i+2}-\mathrm{i}x_{N}x_{1}\gamma_{2N-1}\gamma_{0}. (57)

This observation allows us to reformulate the amplitude evaluation entirely in terms of overlaps between Gaussian states, thereby enabling an efficient implementation within the t-VMC framework. For numerical stability at initialization, we add a small perturbation of order 10−310^{-3} to the parameter θi​j1,2=0\theta^{1,2}_{ij}=0 to ensure that the logarithmic derivatives remain well defined.

Appendix C Details of the spin relaxation problem in the TFIM

We study the real-time dynamics of the total ZZ magnetization 𝒵^=∑i=0N−1Zi\hat{\mathcal{Z}}=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}Z_{i}, starting from a computational-basis product state |𝒙0⟩\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}} under the TFIM Hamiltonian. The time-dependent expectation value is

𝒵⁡(t)=⟨𝒙0|​ei​H^TFIM​(J,h)​t​𝒵^​e−i​H^TFIM​(J,h)​t​|𝒙0⟩.\mathcal{Z}(t)=\bra{{\bm{x}}_{0}}e^{\mathrm{i}\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,h)t}\hat{\mathcal{Z}}e^{-\mathrm{i}\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}(J,h)t}\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}}. (58)

C.1 Exact solution via mapping to Majorana fermions

Using the anticommutation relation {Xi,Zi}=0\{X_{i},Z_{i}\}=0, one obtains Zi​e−i​H^TFIM​(J,h)​t=e−i⁡(H^TFIM​(J,h)−2​h​Xi)​t​Zi,Z_{i}e^{-i\hat{H}_{\mathrm{TFIM}}(J,h)t}=e^{-i\left(\hat{H}_{\mathrm{TFIM}}(J,h)-2hX_{i}\right)t}Z_{i}, which allows us to rewrite

𝒵⁡(t)=∑i⟨𝒙0|​ei​H^​(J,h)​t​e−i⁡(H^​(J,h)−2​h​Xi)​t​Zi​|𝒙0⟩.\begin{split}\mathcal{Z}(t)&=\sum_{i}\bra{{\bm{x}}_{0}}e^{i\hat{H}(J,h)t}e^{-i\left(\hat{H}(J,h)-2hX_{i}\right)t}Z_{i}\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}}.\end{split} (59)

Since |𝒙0⟩\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}} is an eigenstate of every ZiZ_{i} with eigenvalue 𝒙0​(i)∈{±1}{\bm{x}}_{0}(i)\in\{\pm 1\}, we obtain

𝒵⁡(t)=∑i𝒙0​(i)​⟨𝒙0|​ei​H^​(J,h)​t​e−i⁡(H^​(J,h)−2​h​Xi)​t​|𝒙0⟩.\begin{split}\mathcal{Z}(t)=\sum_{i}{\bm{x}}_{0}(i)\,\bra{{\bm{x}}_{0}}e^{i\hat{H}(J,h)t}e^{-i\left(\hat{H}(J,h)-2hX_{i}\right)t}\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}}.\end{split} (60)

To proceed, we decompose the initial state into definite XX-parity sectors, |𝒙0⟩=12​(|𝒙0+⟩+|𝒙0−⟩),\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}^{+}}+\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}^{-}}\right), which yields

𝒵(t)=12∑i𝒙0​(i)​(⟨𝒙0+|​ei​H^​(J,h)​t​e−i⁡(H^​(J,h)−2​h​Xi)​t​|𝒙0+⟩CLOSE+OPEN⟨𝒙0−|​ei​H^​(J,h)​t​e−i⁡(H^​(J,h)−2​h​Xi)​t​|𝒙0−⟩).\begin{split}\mathcal{Z}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}&{\bm{x}}_{0}(i)\Big(\bra{{\bm{x}}_{0}^{+}}e^{i\hat{H}(J,h)t}e^{-i\left(\hat{H}(J,h)-2hX_{i}\right)t}\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}^{+}}\\ +&\bra{{\bm{x}}_{0}^{-}}e^{i\hat{H}(J,h)t}e^{-i\left(\hat{H}(J,h)-2hX_{i}\right)t}\ket{{\bm{x}}_{0}^{-}}\Big).\end{split} (61)

In this form, each contribution has a well-defined XX-parity and can therefore be evaluated efficiently using the Majorana fermionic representation of the TFIM.

C.2 Dressed RBM ansatz and its initialization

In the simulations, we employ a complex RBM with translation symmetry, denoted by ψsymm-RBM​(𝒙)\psi_{\text{symm-RBM}}({\bm{x}}) (see the definition in NetKet [88]). For this symmetric RBM, we fix the visible bias parameter to zero and use a hidden-unit density α=1\alpha=1. When the RBM parameters are initialized close to zero (∼10−3\sim 10^{-3}), the resulting wavefunction ψsymm-RBM​(𝒙)\psi_{\text{symm-RBM}}({\bm{x}}) approximates a uniform superposition over configurations. However, this ansatz alone cannot represent the desired initial state, which has support only on the fully polarized all-down configuration.

To incorporate this structure, we augment the symmetric RBM with a sector-dependent factor fϕ​(𝒙)f_{\bm{\phi}}({\bm{x}}), parameterized by n+1n+1 complex parameters ϕ∈ℂn+1\bm{\phi}\in\mathbb{C}^{n+1}:

ψ𝜽​(𝒙)=fϕ​(𝒙)​ψsymm-RBM​(𝒙),fϕ​(𝒙)=ϕs⁡(𝒙).{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}({\bm{x}})=f_{\bm{\phi}}({\bm{x}})\,\psi_{\text{symm-RBM}}({\bm{x}}),\quad f_{\bm{\phi}}({\bm{x}})=\phi_{s({\bm{x}})}. (62)

Here s⁡(𝒙)≡(∑ixi+n)/2s({\bm{x}})\equiv(\sum_{i}x_{i}+n)/2 denotes the spin sector of configuration 𝒙{\bm{x}}. This construction assigns an independent complex amplitude to each spin sector, allowing the ansatz to selectively enhance or suppress entire sectors. In particular, setting ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1 and ϕs=0\phi_{s}=0 for s≠0s\neq 0 yields a wavefunction supported entirely on the fully polarized all-down configuration 𝒙=(−1,−1,…,−1){\bm{x}}=(-1,-1,\ldots,-1), corresponding to the s=0s=0 sector. In practice, to avoid exact zeros that may lead to numerical instabilities, we initialize ϕs=ϵ=10−5×2−n/2\phi_{s}=\epsilon=10^{-5}\times 2^{-n/2} for s≠0s\neq 0, while fixing ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1 throughout the simulation. Since fϕ​(𝒙)f_{\bm{\phi}}({\bm{x}}) is independent across spin sectors in this parameterization, we refer to it as the uncorrelated parameterization.

To further expose the bias of the quantum geometric tensor, we introduce correlations between different spin sectors in the parameterization. In particular, we couple the single-spin-up sector to another sector, thereby breaking the independence of sector amplitudes. Concretely, we define

fϕ​(𝒙)={ϕ1+ϕ3ifs⁡(𝒙)=3ϕs⁡(𝒙)otherwise,\displaystyle f_{\bm{\phi}}({\bm{x}})=\begin{cases}\phi_{1}+\phi_{3}&\quad\text{if}\quad s({\bm{x}})=3\\ \phi_{s({\bm{x}})}&\quad\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

so that the amplitude of the s=3s=3 sector explicitly depends on ϕ1\phi_{1}, introducing correlations between the s=1s=1 and s=3s=3 sectors. We refer to this as a correlated parameterization.

Under the TFIM Hamiltonian, the resulting state has the following support structure:

supp​(ψ𝜽)\displaystyle{\text{supp}}({\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}) ≈{𝒙∈{±1}n:s⁡(𝒙)=0}\displaystyle\approx\{{\bm{x}}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}:s({\bm{x}})=0\}
supp​(H^TFIM​ψ𝜽)\displaystyle{\text{supp}}(\hat{H}_{\text{TFIM}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}) ≈{𝒙∈{±1}n:s⁡(𝒙)∈{0,1}}\displaystyle\approx\{{\bm{x}}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}:s({\bm{x}})\in\{0,1\}\}
supp​(∂ϕiψ𝜽​(𝒙)​∂ϕjψ𝜽​(𝒙))\displaystyle{\text{supp}}(\partial_{\phi_{i}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}({\bm{x}})\partial_{\phi_{j}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}({\bm{x}})) ={𝒙∈{±1}n}.\displaystyle=\{{\bm{x}}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}\}.

This reveals a pronounced support-mismatch problem both in variational force and QGT estimators. In the following, we give further results to discuss the effectiveness of the blurred sampling method under both parameterizations.

C.3 QGT bias and support of the forces

In this section, we argue why the Hamiltonian-induced blur sampling of Fig. 6(a) still produces the correct dynamics despite the QGT support mismatch problem, and why it fails in Fig. 6(b). In Fig. 7 we calculate the eigenvalue spectrum of the QGT and investigate the support of the force vector in the corresponding eigenbasis. We see in panel (a) that without correlation in the ansatz (first row), the Hamiltonian-induced blur (q2=0q_{2}=0, second column) produces a QGT with extremely limited support, compared to the randomized blur (q2=0.2q_{2}=0.2, first column). This should result in a divergence in the dynamics from the correct result, but we see in Fig. 6(a) that this is not the case. The reason for this can be found in panel (b). We see that both blurred sampling schemes produce unbiased force vectors that are strongly peaked on a single mode for t=0t=0 and t=0.01t=0.01, with the support on other modes having |ρk|<10−8|\rho_{k}|<10^{-8}. Due to this lack support, the bias in the QGT does not affect the final force vector. However, when we look at the same quantities for the correlated ansatz (second row), a different picture emerges. For t=0.01t=0.01, we see that the force vector has significant support on a large number of eigenmodes, which now get amplified incorrectly due to the QGT bias. The consequences are immediate: the dynamics in Fig. 6(b) diverges around this point.

Appendix D Numerical details of t-VMC simulations

The most important part of t-VMC involves the regularization of the 𝑺\bm{S}-matrix in Eq. 2 so that it can be stably inverted. For this, we use the regularizer by Schmitt [9] with the hyperparameters SNRcutoff=2\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{cutoff}}=2, rcond=10−14\texttt{rcond}=10^{-14} and rcond_smooth=10−10\texttt{rcond\_smooth}=10^{-10} for every experiment reported in this work. For sampling, we use Metropolis-Hastings MCMC with local updates depending on the Hamiltonian. In Table 2 we report the hyperparameters of the simulations. We emphasize that these are always kept exactly the same for the experiments with standard sampling and blurred sampling, hence any reported numerics differ only by the sampling scheme used. The code to reproduce all figures in this work can be found at [92]. Finally, we note that the simulations reported in Figures 2,3,4,5(a,b) and 6(a,b) were performed on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 taking at most an hour of wall time. For Figure 5(c) we used 4 NVIDIA H100s, with simulations lasting several hours at most.
